---
title: "Storage, distribution, and hemovigilance"
order: 8
---

## The ticket

Thursday, 3:15 p.m. A unit of leukoreduced Red Blood Cells — O positive, correctly separated,
correctly labeled, release-eligible in Lakeshore Blood Center's inventory since Tuesday — is
pulled for a scheduled shipment to Riverside General Hospital, a fictional 340-bed hospital
forty minutes away that runs no blood collection program of its own and depends entirely on
Lakeshore for red cell supply. The unit rides in a validated shipping container with a
continuous temperature monitor. The courier logs delivery at 4:05 p.m.; the temperature chart
reads in range end to end. Riverside's blood bank receives the unit, logs it into their own
inventory, and it sits there until 9:40 p.m. Friday, when it's issued for a scheduled surgical
patient.

At 9:52 p.m., ten minutes into the transfusion, the patient spikes a fever and starts chilling.
The nurse stops the transfusion — protocol, not overreaction — and Riverside's transfusion
service opens an investigation: what happened, was the product at fault, and who needs to know.

Two separate questions follow, and they don't have the same answer. What does Riverside have to
do about this? And what, if anything, does Lakeshore — a blood center two organizations and one
loading dock removed from the bedside — have to do about it too? Answering both is what this
module is about: everything that happens to a released, correctly labeled unit after module 3
left off, through the hospital, into the patient, and — when something goes wrong — back out
again.

## Why this matters — and the ITSM bridge

The failure mode here isn't subtle: a unit that's correctly typed, correctly labeled, and
correctly released can still hurt a patient if it degrades in transit, or if the transfusion
itself triggers a reaction nobody expected and nobody traces back to its source. Everything
module 3 built — the label, the barcode, the DIN — exists so that when something *does* go
wrong downstream, Lakeshore and Riverside can both answer "which unit, from which donation,
handled how" without guessing. This module is where that traceability actually gets used.

You already run every piece of this, under different names. **Temperature monitoring in storage
and in transit is condition monitoring with alarms and a defined response** — the same shape as
watching a production database's latency dashboard: a threshold breach should trigger an alert
and a documented action, not wait for someone to notice a chart looks off during a routine
review. **A transfusion reaction is the incident** — it happens in real time, at the point of
service, and it demands an immediate operational response (stop the transfusion) independent of
whatever investigation follows. **Hemovigilance reporting — the practice of tracking and
reporting adverse events tied to blood products and transfusions, the term this field uses for
what you'd call incident reporting with an external regulator on the distribution list — is the
notification obligation that fires once the incident is confirmed.** And **traceback — working
backward from a reaction to the donation, and forward again to every other product that donation
produced — is problem management, except it runs against a fixed regulatory clock, not an
internal SLA you set yourselves.**

The sharper point, and the one this scenario is built to surface: **the moment this unit crossed
Lakeshore's loading dock, it crossed into a system Lakeshore doesn't control.** Riverside's
blood bank has its own records, its own staff, its own regulatory obligations as a transfusion
service. That handoff boundary — what data travels with the unit, and what Lakeshore can and
can't see once it's on the other side — isn't a shipping logistics detail. It's a real
governance question, the same one you'd ask about a system that hands a customer record to a
partner's platform: what exactly crossed the boundary, and what happens when something on their
side needs to trace back to something on yours.

## The rule, in plain English

Five things happen, in this order, to a component that's already cleared module 3's bar —
correctly labeled, release-eligible:

1. **Storage and monitoring.** While a unit sits in Lakeshore's inventory, its storage
   temperature has to stay within the product-specific range and has to be recorded — an
   initialed chart, not a memory. This is condition monitoring: a defined range, a continuous
   record, and — operationally, even where the regulation doesn't spell out the word "alarm" —
   a response plan for when the reading drifts.
2. **Shipping.** When a unit moves — Lakeshore to Riverside, or anywhere else — it has to stay
   within a specified temperature range for its product type, for the whole trip, and the
   shipment and its receipt both have to be recorded, tied to the unit's identity, so either
   party can reconstruct who sent what, to whom, and when.
3. **Distribution and receipt.** Lakeshore's shipping record and Riverside's receiving record
   are two halves of the same transaction — this is the exact point where the unit crosses from
   Lakeshore's system of record into Riverside's.
4. **The hospital's own transfusion service.** Once Riverside has the unit, they run their own
   regulated activity before anyone transfuses it: **compatibility testing** — crossmatching the
   unit against the specific patient's blood sample to confirm it won't provoke an immune
   reaction. This is Riverside's job, under Riverside's own CGMP obligations as a transfusion
   service, not Lakeshore's. Lakeshore's part of the story is already done by the time this
   happens; this lesson names it because a Director needs to know this handoff exists, not
   because it's Lakeshore's process to govern.
5. **Transfusion, and — if something goes wrong — reaction investigation and reporting.** The
   nurse administering the unit is the last line of defense and the first to notice a problem.
   What happens after that split into obligations that land differently depending on who's
   involved and how serious it is — the subject of the rest of this module.

Here's where LIS and HIS finally get distinguished properly, because this is the first module
where both organizations' systems are genuinely in play at once. **LIS (Laboratory Information
System)** is the system that manages lab and blood-bank testing workflows — at a hospital, this
is typically what runs compatibility testing, tracks a unit through crossmatch, and holds the
transfusion service's own records. **HIS (Hospital Information System)** is the hospital's
broader clinical and administrative system — patient orders, nursing documentation, the record
of the transfusion actually being administered and what happened during it, often the same
system doctors and nurses know as the EHR (electronic health record). They're not the same
system, and they don't do the same job: the LIS is where "is this unit safe to give this
patient" gets answered; the HIS is where "this patient received this unit, and here's what
happened" gets recorded. A reaction investigation at Riverside typically has to pull from both.

None of this is Lakeshore's system. That's the point. Lakeshore's own system of record — BECS —
stops mattering the moment distribution to Riverside is recorded; everything from Riverside's
receipt forward lives in systems Lakeshore has no visibility into except what specifically comes
back to them. That's the handoff boundary, and it's exactly as real a governance question as
which fields a partner API does and doesn't return.

This is also where BECS earns its fourth and final clause in this course's running definition —
system of record for donor eligibility and deferrals (module 1), gate for quarantine release
(module 2), control over whether a final label can print (module 3), and here: **it drives
inventory, shipping, and final disposition.** That's all this module adds; module 5 puts the
full picture together.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 CFR 600.15 | "Six hundred point one-five" | Blood and blood components must be maintained at a specified temperature range, by product type, during shipment. | The requirement the validated shipping container and its temperature monitor exist to satisfy on Thursday's 40-minute trip to Riverside. |
| 21 CFR 606.165(a)–(c) | "Six-oh-six point one-six-five, paragraphs a through c" | Distribution and receipt procedures must let the shipment or receipt of each unit be readily traced; distribution records (the shipper's side) and receipt records (the receiver's side) each carry defined content, tied to the unit's lot number. | The two-sided record — Lakeshore's shipping entry, Riverside's receiving entry — that marks the exact point the unit crosses from Lakeshore's system into Riverside's. |
| 21 CFR 606.160(b)(3)(iii) | "Six-oh-six point one-six-oh, paragraph b, sub-three, clause iii" | Storage temperature must be recorded, including initialed temperature recorder charts. | Already covered in the first foundation lesson — reused here for the record Lakeshore's own inventory has to produce while this unit sits waiting to ship. |
| 21 CFR 606.170(a) | "Six-oh-six point one-seven-oh, paragraph a" | Adverse reaction complaints and reports require a thorough investigation, written up with conclusions and followup; if the product is found at fault, copies go to the manufacturer or collecting facility. | The rule that puts Riverside's investigation of Friday night's reaction on the record — and the clause that pulls Lakeshore back in if the product turns out to be the cause. |
| 21 CFR 606.170(b) | "Six-oh-six point one-seven-oh, paragraph b" | A fatal complication of blood collection or transfusion must be phoned or electronically reported to FDA's CBER as soon as possible, with a written report within 7 days — filed by the collecting facility for a donor reaction, or by the facility that performed compatibility testing for a transfusion reaction. | The specific, narrow, deadline-driven obligation that would apply if Friday night's reaction had been fatal — and, notice, it would be Riverside's obligation to file, not Lakeshore's, because Riverside performed the compatibility testing. |

## The actual text

Start with the shipping temperature requirement, quoted verbatim from `sources/cfr/600.15.md`
(retrieved from eCFR):

> The following products shall be maintained during shipment at the specified temperatures:
>
> ...Red Blood Cells (liquid product): Between 1 and 10 °C.

That's a two-degree-wide floor and an eight-degree-wide ceiling, for the whole trip — not an
average, not a "mostly in range." Thursday's shipping container and its continuous monitor exist
specifically to prove that range held from Lakeshore's dock to Riverside's receiving desk.

Now the two-sided record that marks the handoff itself, quoted verbatim from
`sources/cfr/606.165.md`:

> (a) Distribution and receipt procedures shall include a system by which the distribution or
> receipt of each unit can be readily determined to facilitate its recall, if necessary.
>
> (b) Distribution records shall contain information to readily facilitate the identification of
> the name and address of the consignee, the date and quantity delivered, the lot number of the
> unit(s), the date of expiration or the date of collection, whichever is applicable, or for
> crossmatched blood and blood components, the name of the recipient.
>
> (c) Receipt records shall contain the name and address of the collecting facility, date
> received, donor or lot number assigned by the collecting facility and the date of expiration or
> the date of collection, whichever is applicable.

Read (b) and (c) side by side and notice what they don't share: Lakeshore's distribution record
carries the consignee's name and address and the delivered quantity; Riverside's receipt record
carries the collecting facility's name and address and the date received. Both sides carry the
lot number — the thing that actually ties them together — but each record is built for its own
side of the transaction, not a shared, jointly-owned record either party can query the other's
half of. That's the LIS/HIS boundary in regulatory form: the lot number crosses, a defined slice
of metadata crosses with it, and everything else — Riverside's crossmatch results, its nursing
documentation, whatever its own LIS and HIS capture about this specific patient — stays entirely
inside systems 606.165 never requires Lakeshore to see.

Lakeshore's own storage-side obligation while this unit waited to ship, already established in
the first foundation lesson from `sources/cfr/606.160.md`:

> (iii) Storage temperature, including initialed temperature recorder charts.

Now the record that actually gets generated once Friday night's reaction happens, quoted
verbatim from `sources/cfr/606.170.md`:

> (a) Records shall be maintained of any reports of complaints of adverse reactions regarding
> each unit of blood or blood product arising as a result of blood collection or transfusion. A
> thorough investigation of each reported adverse reaction shall be made. A written report of the
> investigation of adverse reactions, including conclusions and followup, shall be prepared and
> maintained as part of the record for that lot or unit of final product by the collecting or
> transfusing facility. When it is determined that the product was at fault in causing a
> transfusion reaction, copies of all such written reports shall be forwarded to and maintained by
> the manufacturer or collecting facility.

Read that last sentence carefully, because it's the answer to this module's opening question.
Riverside runs the investigation — they're the "transfusing facility." But if that investigation
concludes the product itself was at fault, the regulation requires the report to come back to
Lakeshore — "the manufacturer or collecting facility" — and Lakeshore has to maintain it. The
obligation doesn't stop at Riverside's door just because Riverside did the transfusing.

And the narrower, harder-deadline obligation that would have applied if this had gone worse,
quoted verbatim from the same source:

> (b) When a complication of blood collection or transfusion is confirmed to be fatal, the
> Director, Office of Compliance and Biologics Quality, CBER, must be notified by telephone,
> facsimile, express mail, or electronically transmitted mail as soon as possible. A written
> report of the investigation must be submitted to the Director, Office of Compliance and
> Biologics Quality, CBER... within 7 days after the fatality by the collecting facility in the
> event of a donor reaction, or by the facility that performed the compatibility tests in the
> event of a transfusion reaction.

Notice who reports what. A *donor* reaction fatality is reported by the collecting facility —
Lakeshore, if this had happened during Tuesday's draw. A *transfusion* reaction fatality is
reported by whoever performed the compatibility testing — Riverside, not Lakeshore, because
Riverside is the one who ran the crossmatch this module's rule-in-plain-English section named
above. Same regulation, same 7-day clock, two entirely different filers depending on which side
of the DIN's lifecycle the fatality happened on.

One more obligation exists and is deliberately not re-taught here: if Riverside's investigation
turns up something that looks like a manufacturing or process deviation on Lakeshore's side —
not just an unlucky immune reaction, but an actual gap in how the unit was collected, processed,
or handled — that can trigger Lakeshore's own biological product deviation reporting obligation
under 21 CFR 606.171, on its own 45-day clock. The risk-and-controls-vocabulary foundation
lesson already covered exactly how that reportability determination works and what "may affect"
means in that section's text. This lesson doesn't re-derive it — just flags that this is the
door 606.170(a)'s "copies... forwarded to" clause can open.

## What an inspector would actually look for

An FDA investigator or AABB assessor reconstructing Friday night's reaction doesn't ask either
organization to narrate what happened. They ask for specific records, on both sides of the
loading dock.

**Lakeshore's shipping record and Riverside's receipt record**, matched against each other by lot
number, per 606.165(b) and (c) — proof the handoff itself is traceable, not just remembered.

**The temperature chart covering the unit's time in Lakeshore's inventory and its time in
transit** — the initialed storage chart under 606.160(b)(3)(iii) plus whatever continuous
monitoring record the shipping container produced against 600.15's range. A gap here doesn't
just raise a documentation question; it removes the evidence that would rule the product itself
in or out as a cause of Friday night's reaction.

**Riverside's own compatibility testing and adverse reaction investigation records**, which an
FDA investigator visiting *Riverside* — a separate inspection, under Riverside's own registration
as a transfusion service — would ask for directly, not through Lakeshore. And if that
investigation concludes the product was at fault, **the copy of that report that 606.170(a)
requires be forwarded to and maintained by Lakeshore** — a bad answer here sounds like "we never
heard back from the hospital," because the regulation doesn't make that outcome optional.

A bad answer to "how do you know what happened to this unit between your dock and the patient"
sounds like "the hospital would have called us if it mattered." That's a hope resting on another
organization's goodwill, not a control. The control an inspector expects to see is the paired
distribution/receipt record plus a documented adverse-reaction forwarding process that doesn't
depend on Riverside remembering to pick up the phone.

## Common traps

**"Once it ships, it's the hospital's problem."** This is the trap the whole scenario is built to
break. Lakeshore's manufacturing responsibility for the unit is largely done at distribution —
but 606.170(a)'s forwarding requirement means Lakeshore's *record-keeping and reportability*
obligations don't end at the loading dock. If Riverside's investigation implicates the product,
that finding has to come back to Lakeshore, get maintained, and potentially feed a 606.171 BPDR
determination on Lakeshore's own clock. "Not our problem anymore" is exactly the wrong instinct
the moment an investigation names your product as a possible cause.

**"The hospital's transfusion service is basically an extension of Lakeshore's quality system."**
Wrong in the opposite direction. Riverside's compatibility testing, its LIS, its HIS
documentation of the transfusion — none of it is Lakeshore's system, SOP, or regulatory
obligation to govern. Riverside is a separately regulated transfusion service, inspected on its
own cycle, filing its own 606.170(b) fatality report if one's ever needed. Treating Riverside's
process as something Lakeshore's Quality Analyst should audit directly is a scope error; the real
point of leverage is the paired record at the handoff, not oversight of what happens after it.

## What this means for your job

- **Ask whether your shipping process treats temperature monitoring as condition monitoring with
  a defined alert-and-response plan, or just as a chart someone reviews after the fact.** 600.15
  sets the range; it doesn't by itself guarantee anyone notices a breach in time to act on it —
  that gap is a process question worth asking your Quality Analyst directly.
- **When a reaction gets reported by a hospital, ask immediately whether 606.170(a)'s forwarding
  requirement has actually been triggered and honored** — don't wait for the hospital to
  volunteer a copy of their investigation. If your process depends on the hospital remembering to
  send it, that's a gap you own, not one you can hand off.
- **Know which fatality-reporting clock applies before assuming it's yours.** A donor-reaction
  fatality is Lakeshore's 7-day filing under 606.170(b); a transfusion-reaction fatality is the
  compatibility-testing facility's filing — usually the hospital's. Confusing the two wastes the
  narrow window either deadline gives you.
- **Treat the distribution/receipt record pair, not a phone call, as your actual traceability
  control across the LIS/HIS boundary.** If Lakeshore's system and a hospital's system can
  disagree about which lot number went where, that's the same data-integrity gap this course has
  flagged from module 1 onward, just at the last handoff instead of the first.
- **Don't confuse "the hospital's transfusion service does this too" with "Lakeshore governs
  this too."** Crossmatching, HIS documentation, and Riverside's own investigation process are
  real, regulated activities — just not activities your Quality Analyst reports on or Lakeshore's
  SOPs control.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Thursday's temperature chart shows the unit stayed in range the entire 40-minute trip to Riverside. Does that fact alone close out any regulatory question this scenario raises?

No — and this is worth being precise about. The in-range chart satisfies 600.15's shipping
temperature requirement and gives Lakeshore its half of the traceability record under 606.165.
But it says nothing about what happens next: Riverside's compatibility testing, the transfusion
itself, and Friday night's reaction are separate events governed by separate parts of this
module's rule. A clean shipping record rules out one possible cause of the reaction (a
temperature-related product problem) — it doesn't close the investigation, and it doesn't touch
606.170(a)'s requirement that the reaction itself still be investigated and documented.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Friday night's reaction turns out to be non-fatal — the patient recovers fully after the transfusion is stopped. Does 21 CFR 606.170 require Lakeshore to independently notify FDA about it?

No — and this is one of those places where the honest answer is "there's no regulatory
requirement here," not "yes, cite the rule." 606.170(b)'s FDA notification and 7-day written
report only apply when a complication is *confirmed to be fatal*. A non-fatal reaction still
triggers 606.170(a)'s investigation-and-record requirement — Riverside has to investigate and
document it, and forward a copy to Lakeshore if the product is found at fault — but that's an
internal record-keeping and forwarding obligation, not an FDA notification. Treating every
reaction as automatically FDA-reportable overstates the rule in exactly the direction the
regulatory-landscape-orientation foundation lesson warned against.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: Riverside's nurse documents that she stopped the transfusion at 9:52 p.m. and recorded the patient's vitals. Is that entry most likely captured in Riverside's LIS or their HIS?

Most likely the HIS (Hospital Information System) — the clinical/administrative system where
nursing documentation, orders, and the record of what happened during patient care actually live,
often the same system staff call the EHR. Riverside's LIS (Laboratory Information System) is
where the blood bank side lives: the compatibility testing and crossmatch results that cleared
this unit for this patient before the transfusion started. A full reaction investigation
typically has to pull from both systems — the LIS to confirm what was tested and matched, the HIS
to confirm what actually happened at the bedside — which is exactly why the boundary between
those two systems matters the moment an investigation needs to reconstruct the full picture.
:::

processing and labeling, and now storage, distribution, the hospital handoff, and what has to
happen when something goes wrong afterward. Module 5, `becs-in-the-pipeline` — the last module of
this course — goes back over this exact same ground, but with the systems lens on: every place
BECS touched this pipeline, gathered into one picture, and why FDA treats it as a different kind
of software than anything else your organization runs.
